searches.note: Twenty five searches of a share of twenty eight, three left unspent, none of them the author's. Nine were restricted to a house's own domain (bvwines.com twice, heitzcellar.com once, stagsleapwinecellars.com twice, montelena.com once, opusonewinery.com three times) and are read as primary through their summaries; nine kept the house's own domain out, and where the author had leant on them Wikipedia and Decanter, so that the second source would be independent; seven went to the open web. The one shared search is the Paris tasting of 1976, which three records tell. No WebFetch was tried.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the classification, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

The making, the blend and the sites went first to the house's own domain, read through its search summaries; the history then went to the open web with the house's domain, and where the author had used them Wikipedia and Decanter, kept out, so that each date found its second source elsewhere.

Where a search contradicted the record it was set right with its source; where a detail was found in no source of this check it was cut or said with less (the year of the switch to French oak at Beaulieu, the rootstock and the year of the Heitz replanting, the war as the end of the Tubbs family's winemaking, the twenty one years of the Cask 23 letter, the fifteen months of Opus One in bottle).

The dead are named with dates where two sources agree; Georges de Latour and Joe Heitz stay dated by their deaths alone, and the grower of FAY, the founders' wives, the couples who owned Martha's Vineyard and the Chateau of 1958, and every living person stay described.

Sources whose title or address names a living person or carries a score were met among the results (a winemaker's interview, a critic's own site, a guide with a writer's name in its address, a house's product page and a magazine headline with points) and are cited neither in the fragment nor here. The fragment's sources were not changed; the sources of this check are listed per change and per record.

tested: Founded 1900, the first land at Rutherford bought by the founder and his wife, the name from her beau lieu: the library's year, a merchant's page and the Napa Valley Register; one account dates the winery to 1903. Confirmed as the land of 1900.
Prohibition and the altar wine: Cult Wine's collection page and an essay on the sacramental loophole give the same, beside the house. Confirmed; the hedge is kept, though no longer needed.

Tchelistcheff brought from France in 1938, his tasting of the family's 1936 and its release about 1940 under the founder's name, the year he died: a merchant's page, an interview with the house and the house's history; one house page gives 1941. Confirmed, about 1940 kept.

Ranch No. 1 and Ranch No. 2 on the western bench of Rutherford, planted by the founder in the early 1900s: the house's pages (Ranch No. 1 around the original estate, bought 1903; Ranch No. 2 on the southern Rutherford bench, 1907 or 1910). Confirmed.

The making: part fermented in new French oak barrels, the rest in stainless steel and concrete tanks, the malolactic and the ageing in barrel, twenty one or twenty two months, ninety to ninety five per cent new: the house's sheets for 2015, 2018, 2021, 2022 and 2023. Confirmed.
Grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon with five to nine per cent Petit Verdot in 2021 to 2023 and Merlot or Malbec in earlier years, by the house's sheets. Confirmed.

American oak until 1989: Decanter's 1989 stands against a cellar list's half French 1991 and first new French 1992, and one blog says the first vintages were in French oak before the war. Not settled; said with less.
Other wines: the Reserve Ranch 1 Rutherford Cabernet Sauvignon (Cabernet with Petit Verdot, the property around the original estate) and the Rutherford Cabernet, on the house's pages. Confirmed.
Georges de Latour's dates: born 1856 in one merchant's page beside the author's two weak sources; dead 1940 in four. He stays dated by his death.

The questions: the wine question's Ranches against Howell Mountain, Carneros and Sonoma, one right answer, each wrong one a real Napa or Sonoma place; the story question's Tchelistcheff against three dead winemakers of the same years, the exp naming Heitz under him. Sound.
The rules: nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, British, no dash. Sound.

changed.was: Until 1989 the wine was aged in American oak.
changed.now: For decades it was aged in American oak, until French barrels came in around 1990.
changed.why: Decanter gives 1989; a restaurant's cellar list gives the 1991 as aged half in French and half in American oak and the 1992 as the first with new French barrels, about a third; no single year can stand.

tested: Founded 1961, a small vineyard of mostly Grignolino and a basic winery south of St Helena bought by Joe Heitz and his wife: The Wine Independent, Decanter's profile and Wine-Searcher. Confirmed.
The move of 1964 to Spring Valley east of the town, to a property with a stone cellar of 1898: three accounts give 1898, one 1868. Confirmed as 1898.
Heitz at Beaulieu under Tchelistcheff in the 1950s, then Fresno State, where he set up the teaching of winemaking: The Wine Independent and Decanter (hired 1951, left 1957 or 1958). Confirmed.

The handshake of 1965 with the couple who bought the vineyard in 1963, the 1965 fruit in the regular bottling, the first bottling under the vineyard's name with the 1966: Wine-Searcher, Grape Collective and a merchant's listing of the 1966. Confirmed, and the story set right (below).
The first Napa wine labelled by vineyard: the house's claim, repeated by Grape Collective and Wine-Searcher. Kept, hedged.
The 1970 at the Paris tasting of 1976: Wikipedia's table of the tasting lists it among the reds. Confirmed.

No Martha's Vineyard from 1993 to 1995 after phylloxera: two outside guides and listings give the gap and the replanting, Wikipedia the mid 1990s. Confirmed; the rootstock and the year of replanting found in none.

The making: a year in neutral oak tanks, about three years in new Limousin barrels and a year in bottle on the house's 2013 sheet; four years in French oak vessels of many sizes and two in bottle on its 2014 sheet. The record's wording, varied from vintage to vintage, stands, and the wine question's key matches the house's usual regime.

The sale of 2018: the Napa Valley Register, The Drinks Business and Wein.plus, which add that the vineyard stayed with its owners and the grape contract stayed in place. Confirmed; the buyer is living and stays unnamed.
Joe Heitz's death in 2000: not searched again; the author's house page and Decanter stand.

The questions: the wine question's regime against American oak, steel and old casks, each wrong in a way the exp names; the story question's Beaulieu against Inglenook, Charles Krug and Schramsberg. Sound.
The rules: nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, British, no dash. Sound.

tested: Founded 1970, the ranch next to the grower's bought and planted as S.L.V.: Benchland's district guide and Grape Collective beside the library. Confirmed.
The grower's planting of 1961, the first Cabernet of what became the district: Wine Spectator's obituary, the Napa Valley Wine Academy and Benchland. Confirmed; the hedge stays.

The tasting of the grower's homemade wine in 1969: Grape Collective gives the visit as about 1969 and the wine as a 1968, the Napa Valley Register a 1968 and The Happy Vine a 1969. Said with less (below).
24 May 1976, the 1973 first among the reds ahead of Mouton Rothschild 1970: Wikipedia's table of the tasting and its record of averaged marks, with NPR as the author had it. Confirmed.
Cask 23 from the harvest of 1974, a lot of S.L.V. found distinct while tasting with Tchelistcheff and named for the large wooden cask: the house's past vintages page and a merchant. Confirmed.

FAY bought in 1986 and first in Cask 23 with the 1990: the house's page (the 1990 the first to include Fay grapes, only the tenth Cask 23) and a merchant (Cask 23 a blend of the two from 1990). Confirmed; the twenty one years cut (below).

The making: fermented in steel, ten per cent in new barrels with the heads off in 2016, twenty to twenty one and a half months in French oak, ninety five to a hundred per cent new, by the house's sheets of 2012, 2014, 2016, 2022 and 2023. Confirmed.
The grapes: none but Cabernet in 2016 and 2022, a touch of Cabernet Franc in 2023, Merlot in the 1979 by a merchant's listing. Said wider (below).
The label: the house's labels of 1993 and 1995 and its sheets print Napa Valley; the early labels say red table wine, the later ones Cabernet Sauvignon. The record's Napa Valley stands.
The sale of 2007 to Ste. Michelle Wine Estates and the Antinori family: not searched again; it rests on the author's sources and the library.

The questions: the wine question's S.L.V. and FAY against To Kalon and Martha's Vineyard, the Rutherford bench and Howell Mountain; the story question's 1986 against 1961, 1970 and 1990, each a real date of the record. Sound.
The rules: nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, British, no dash. Sound.

tested: Founded 1882, Alfred L. Tubbs (1827 to 1896) and his land north of Calistoga at the foot of Mount Saint Helena: the National Register's listing, Wikipedia's Alfred L. Tubbs and the Napa Wine Project; one account dates the first vintage to 1886. Confirmed.

The stone château and the winery's size by his death: the National Register's listing gives a stone winery of about 1888 and, in the 1890s, the largest winery in Calistoga and one of the largest in Napa County. Confirmed.

The grandson's revival after Prohibition in 1933: two accounts. Confirmed. The family's end of winemaking by the end of the Second World War: one summary says the winery closed again on the grandson's death in 1947. Cut (below).
The sale of 1958 to a couple who dug Jade Lake and laid out a Chinese garden: Grape Experiences and Winervana. Confirmed; the couple stay described.
The purchase of 1972 by Jim Barrett and partners and the hiring of Grgich: two accounts. Confirmed.

The 1973 Chardonnay: malolactic blocked by Grgich (the Napa Wine Project and a reprint of Decanter's Wine Legend on another winery's site); most of the fruit from Sonoma County (the Napa Wine Project: the majority; a breakdown on another site with Belle Terre, Bacigalupi and Hanna, one placing Bacigalupi wrongly in Oak Knoll). Confirmed; a little from Napa set right (below).
24 May 1976, first among the whites ahead of a Meursault Charmes; a bottle at the Smithsonian: Wikipedia's table and the Smithsonian's own object page. Confirmed.

The present Chardonnay: no malolactic, about ten months in French oak, ten per cent new on the 2013 sheet, by the house's sheets of 2013, 2018 to 2021 and 2024; drawn from Napa, the Sonoma wine bottled apart as a Russian River Valley Chardonnay from 2022. Confirmed; a small share new stands.
Montelena a contraction of Mount Saint Helena: two accounts. Confirmed.

The questions: the wine question's no malolactic against steel, Carneros and Sauvignon Blanc, the exp teaching malic and lactic acid; the story question's Sonoma against the estate, Carneros and Oakville. Sound.
The rules: nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, British, no dash. Sound.

tested: The meeting in Hawaii in 1970, the agreement at Mouton in 1978, the 1979 made at the Robert Mondavi Winery, the announcement of 1980 and the release of the 1979 and 1980 together in 1984: This Day in Wine History, The Wine Cellar Insider and a merchant. Confirmed.

The winery: ground broken in July 1989 and finished in October 1991, just in time for harvest, the 1991 the first wine made entirely there, by the estate's own pages and its 1991 notes, and inaugurated by the Baron's daughter by an outside account. Confirmed.

The four parcels in the west of Oakville, two within To Kalon and the Ballestra and River parcels around the winery, alluvial soils at the foot of the Mayacamas, gravel giving way to clay and silt towards the river: the estate's own pages. Confirmed.
The barrel time: seventeen to nineteen and a half months in new French oak by the estate's pages for 2017 to 2022. Confirmed as about a year and a half.
The bottle time and the release: fifteen months and the first of October in two accounts, eighteen months in one guide, a year and a half on one merchant's sheet. Said with less (below).
Overture: first made in 1993, a blend of several vintages until the 2021, the first vintage dated bottling, by the estate's notes and a merchant. Set right (below).
Constellation's purchase of the Mondavi company in 2004 and the Baron's daughter carrying on: not searched again; they rest on the author's sources.
The questions: the wine question's Bordeaux blend against Syrah, Merlot led and Cabernet alone; the story question's 1984 against 1981, a year after harvest and 1991. Sound.
The rules: nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, British, no dash. Sound.
